title: Large-Scale Spectral Graph Neural Networks via Laplacian Sparsification

problem.claim: Spectral GNNs do not scale well to large graphs because learning polynomial coefficients requires multiple forward propagation executions.

gap.claim: Existing scaling approaches can disrupt end-to-end training, potentially affect performance, and become impractical with high-dimensional input features.

contributions.claim: SGNN-LS uses Laplacian sparsification to approximate the propagation patterns of spectral GNNs.
The method generates Laplacian sparsifiers that approximate fixed and learnable polynomial filters with theoretical guarantees.
The method supports linear layers on input node features, enabling end-to-end training and processing of raw text features.

stated_novelty.claim: The authors explicitly describe SGNN-LS as a novel graph spectral sparsification method.

author_reported_evidence.claim: The authors report an extensive experimental analysis across datasets with varied graph scales and properties.
The authors report superior efficiency and effectiveness compared with corresponding approximated base models.
The authors report especially strong results on Ogbn-papers100M, with 111M nodes and 1.6B edges, and MAG-scholar-C, with 2.8M features.

narrative_sequence.summary: GNNs are important for representation learning in graph-based tasks, and polynomial-filter spectral GNNs perform promisingly on homophilous and heterophilous graphs.
Spectral GNN scalability is limited by repeated forward propagation executions needed to learn polynomial coefficients.
Removing input-feature linear layers can disrupt end-to-end training, affect performance, and be impractical for high-dimensional features.
SGNN-LS applies Laplacian sparsification to approximate spectral GNN propagation, with guarantees for fixed and learnable polynomial filters.
The method retains input linear layers and is evaluated across graph datasets, with reported advantages on particularly large or high-dimensional datasets.

source_observation.claim: The authors report benefits on a graph with 111M nodes and 1.6B edges and on a dataset with 2.8M features.

interpretation.claim: The approach is intended to address both graph-scale and feature-dimensionality challenges.

application.claim: Large-scale graph applications with raw text or other high-dimensional node features may be candidate settings for this method.

exception.claim: The abstract does not establish performance across all graph types or quantify the reported efficiency and effectiveness gains.

unknowns: The abstract does not provide algorithmic details or sparsifier construction costs.
The abstract does not report quantitative metrics, baselines beyond corresponding approximated base models, or statistical uncertainty.
The abstract does not specify the exact theoretical assumptions or approximation bounds.
